summary: Renames the three-bit EXP field in the MPLS label stack entry to Traffic Class, since it is now used as a class of service marker rather than being experimental. It updates many earlier RFCs for consistent naming. This is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: The MPLS field once called EXP is renamed Traffic Class. The field remains three bits and occupies the same place in the label stack entry.

subtitle: MPLS renames its three-bit EXP field to Traffic Class.

tldr.problem: The MPLS label stack's three-bit EXP field was described as experimental, although standards defined its use for traffic classification.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC renames the field to Traffic Class and updates references in earlier MPLS documents.
tldr.outcome: The packet format and field size stay the same; the name clarifies the field's use. The RFC updates 13 earlier RFCs.

today: RFC 5462 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2009. It updates 13 earlier MPLS RFCs, including RFC 3032.

sections.title: Why EXP Was Renamed
sections.content:
RFC 3032 defined a three-bit field in the MPLS label stack entry and called it EXP, describing it as reserved for experimental use. The field was intended to carry class-of-service information, but its use was not settled when RFC 3032 was published.

Later standards defined uses for traffic classification and explicit congestion marking. Calling it Traffic Class better describes those uses and discourages assumptions that the field is available for unrelated purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: The old name suggested that the field was open for experiments. The new name says that it carries traffic-class information.

sections.title: Changes to Earlier RFCs
sections.content:
RFC 5462 changes the relevant text and figure in RFC 3032 to call the field Traffic Class (TC). In RFC 3270 and RFC 5129, references to EXP now refer to TC, and their text is adjusted to use the new name.

The RFC also updates other documents that refer to the EXP field, including RFCs 3272, 3443, 3469, 3564, 3985, 4182, 4364, 4379, 4448, and 4761. References to EXP bits in IETF documents now mean the TC field.
sections.plainLanguage: The updated RFCs use TC where they previously said EXP. This is a terminology change that reflects the field's established role.

sections.title: What the Rename Changes
sections.content:
The field's name changes wherever earlier documents call it the EXP field, EXP bits, or a similar form. For most updated RFCs, only the name of the label-stack field changes.

The actual bits on the wire remain unchanged. This RFC does not introduce a new encoding or alter the width or position of the field.
sections.plainLanguage: The field stays in the same place and carries the same bits. Only the name and the explanation of its purpose change.

sections.title: Use of the Traffic Class Field
sections.content:
The Traffic Class field is used for quality-of-service and explicit congestion notification functions. Because it has only three bits, these functions may rewrite some or all of the field.

Implementations may examine the field with or without label context. When a new label stack entry is pushed, the TC value may be copied so entries have consistent traffic-class values.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks use TC information to handle traffic classes and congestion. The field may be updated as packets pass through the network.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC changes only the name of one field in the MPLS shim header. It states that the change introduces no new security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The field's name changes, but packet behavior does not. The RFC identifies no new security issue from the rename.
